summary.title: Go at Google: Language Design in the Service of Software Engineering
summary.one_liner: Rob Pike's SPLASH 2012 keynote explains how Go's design (explicit dependencies, no unused or circular imports, export data in object files, package paths) targets slow builds and large-scale software engineering at Google.
takeaways: Go makes unused imports a compile-time error and forbids circular imports, so the dependency graph stays precise and minimal.
Compilers read one object file per import containing export data, rather than re-reading header files, which is why Go builds are much faster than C/C++.
C's #ifndef include guards scale poorly: a single header can be read dozens of times per compilation, and it is hard to know which includes are still needed.
Package paths must be unique while package names need not be, and remote packages are fetched by URL-based paths using go get.
Go's design favors clarity and tooling (small regular grammar, parseable without type info) over research novelty.
summary.summary: Rob Pike's modified keynote from SPLASH 2012 argues that Go was built to solve software engineering problems at Google, such as slow builds, uncontrolled C/C++ dependencies, and scale. He walks through how C's preprocessor include model and C++ headers cause massive redundant work, using measured examples like 8 GB of expanded input from 4.2 MB of source. He then shows how Go's explicit, checked imports, single-file export data, banned circular imports, path-based package naming, and regular syntax make compilation fast and tooling easier. The article is an essay with code snippets and concrete build-time measurements rather than a hands-on tutorial.
